blocks.en: 🌱 Practical Theology — Unit 4: Prayer I — What Prayer Is
blocks.es_reference: 🌱 Teología Práctica — Unidad 4: La Oración I — Qué Es la Oración

blocks.en: Professors: Dr. Wayne Cook & Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesores: Dr. Wayne Cook y Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: Introduction: At the Center of Our Time with God
blocks.es_reference: Introducción: En el Centro de Nuestro Tiempo con Dios

blocks.en: We have learned to walk with God and to keep a daily time with Him. At the center of that time is prayer. But what is prayer, really? Many think of it as simply asking God for things, and others as the saying of certain religious words. It is far more than either. In this unit we ask three questions: what is prayer, how did the Lord Jesus teach us to pray, and what kinds of prayer does the Bible give us? The next unit will carry us further — into prayer in Scripture, praying together as a church, and fasting.
blocks.es_reference: Hemos aprendido a andar con Dios y a guardar un tiempo diario con Él. En el centro de ese tiempo está la oración. Pero ¿qué es la oración, en realidad? Muchos la piensan como sencillamente pedirle cosas a Dios, y otros como el decir ciertas palabras religiosas. Es mucho más que cualquiera de las dos. En esta unidad hacemos tres preguntas: ¿qué es la oración, cómo nos enseñó a orar el Señor Jesús, y qué clases de oración nos da la Biblia? La unidad siguiente nos llevará más adelante — a la oración en la Escritura, a orar juntos como iglesia, y al ayuno.

blocks.en: I. What Prayer Is — More Than a Conversation, Yet Like One
blocks.es_reference: I. Qué Es la Oración — Más Que una Conversación, y Sin Embargo Como Una

blocks.en: Some say prayer is simply a conversation. It is much more than that. Dr. Ted Rogers, who teaches a course on prayer at our church, offers this careful definition: prayer is to initiate communication with God for the purpose of intercession, supplication, praise, confession, and thanksgiving, with worshipful intent — communication that draws us closer to God and, for that moment, even sets us in the place of one who stands before Him for others. Notice three things in that definition. Prayer is initiated by us toward God: it is not chanting, nor thanking "the universe," nor speaking to any created thing, for the universe is made but God is self-existent. Already in the days of Enosh "men began to call on the name of the Lord" (Genesis 4:26, NKJV). Prayer is directed to God, with worshipful intent. And prayer changes us as we pray.
blocks.es_reference: Algunos dicen que la oración es sencillamente una conversación. Es mucho más que eso. El Dr. Ted Rogers, quien enseña un curso sobre la oración en nuestra iglesia, ofrece esta definición cuidadosa: la oración es iniciar comunicación con Dios con el propósito de intercesión, súplica, alabanza, confesión y gratitud, con intención de adoración — comunicación que nos acerca más a Dios y, por ese momento, hasta nos pone en el lugar de quien se presenta delante de Él por otros. Note tres cosas en esa definición. La oración es iniciada por nosotros hacia Dios: no es repetir cánticos, ni dar gracias al "universo", ni hablarle a cosa creada alguna, pues el universo es hecho, mas Dios es el que existe por sí mismo. Ya en los días de Enós "los hombres comenzaron a invocar el nombre de Jehová" (Génesis 4:26, RVG). La oración se dirige a Dios, con intención de adoración. Y la oración nos cambia al orar.

blocks.en: Yet though prayer is far more than mere conversation, it is meant to be carried on like one — like a conversation between friends. If we pictured the Lord Jesus sitting in a chair before us, we would not reach for stiff, artificial words; we would speak to Him plainly, as to a friend who loves us. (It is worth remembering that when the King James Bible was written, "thee, thy, and thou" were the everyday, informal words, while "you" was the formal speech of royalty. Today that is reversed — yet many of us still reach for old, formal-sounding words when we pray, as though God preferred a special religious language. He does not. Speak to Him honestly, in your own words.) And because prayer is a kind of conversation, we must also listen. "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psalm 46:10, NKJV). Do not be afraid of silence in prayer; God Himself may at that moment be speaking to you.
blocks.es_reference: Sin embargo, aunque la oración es mucho más que mera conversación, está destinada a llevarse a cabo como una — como una conversación entre amigos. Si imagináramos al Señor Jesús sentado en una silla delante de nosotros, no buscaríamos palabras rígidas y artificiales; le hablaríamos con sencillez, como a un amigo que nos ama. (Vale la pena recordar que cuando se escribió la Biblia King James, "thee, thy y thou" eran las palabras cotidianas e informales del inglés, mientras que "you" era el habla formal de la realeza. Hoy eso se ha invertido — y aun así muchos de nosotros todavía buscamos palabras antiguas y de sonido formal cuando oramos, como si Dios prefiriera un lenguaje religioso especial. No es así. Háblele con honestidad, en sus propias palabras.) Y puesto que la oración es una especie de conversación, también debemos escuchar. "Estad quietos, y conoced que yo soy Dios" (Salmos 46:10, RVG). No tema al silencio en la oración; Dios mismo podría en ese momento estar hablándole.

blocks.en: II. How Jesus Taught Us to Pray: The Lord's Prayer
blocks.es_reference: II. Cómo Nos Enseñó Jesús a Orar: El Padre Nuestro

blocks.en: When His disciples wanted to learn to pray, Jesus gave them a model. He had just warned, "when you pray, do not use vain repetitions as the heathen do" (Matthew 6:7, NKJV) — so the Lord's Prayer is not a set of magic words to be repeated mechanically, but a pattern to follow. "In this manner, therefore, pray: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come. Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one" (Matthew 6:9–13, NKJV).
blocks.es_reference: Cuando sus discípulos quisieron aprender a orar, Jesús les dio un modelo. Acababa de advertir: "orando, no uséis vanas repeticiones, como los gentiles" (Mateo 6:7, RVG) — así que el Padre Nuestro no es un conjunto de palabras mágicas que se repiten mecánicamente, sino un patrón a seguir. "Vosotros, pues, oraréis así: Padre nuestro que estás en el cielo, santificado sea tu nombre. Venga tu reino. Hágase tu voluntad, como en el cielo, así también en la tierra. El pan nuestro de cada día, dánoslo hoy. Y perdónanos nuestras deudas, como también nosotros perdonamos a nuestros deudores. Y no nos metas en tentación, mas líbranos del mal" (Mateo 6:9–13, RVG).

blocks.en: Walk slowly through it. "Our Father" uses the word abba, the most intimate family word of that day — we come as a trusting child to a loving father; yet "hallowed be Your name" reminds us He is holy, set apart, utterly unique. Intimacy and reverence held together. "Your kingdom come, Your will be done" — before we ask anything for ourselves, we put God's kingdom and will first. "Give us this day our daily bread" — only now, halfway through, comes the first request for ourselves, and even it teaches us to depend on God as our Provider day by day. "Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors" — our debts are our sins, and our being forgiven is tied to our forgiving others. "Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us" — a plea that God would keep us and rescue us. Notice the order, for it is the opposite of how many are taught: adoration and God's will come first; our own needs and our confession come after. We do not begin with our shopping list, but with our God.
blocks.es_reference: Recórralo despacio. "Padre nuestro" usa la palabra abba, la palabra familiar más íntima de aquel día — venimos como un hijo que confía a un padre que ama; sin embargo, "santificado sea tu nombre" nos recuerda que Él es santo, apartado, completamente único. Intimidad y reverencia unidas. "Venga tu reino, hágase tu voluntad" — antes de pedir algo para nosotros, ponemos primero el reino y la voluntad de Dios. "El pan nuestro de cada día, dánoslo hoy" — solo ahora, a la mitad, viene la primera petición para nosotros, y aun ella nos enseña a depender de Dios como nuestro Proveedor día tras día. "Perdónanos nuestras deudas, como también nosotros perdonamos" — nuestras deudas son nuestros pecados, y el ser perdonados está ligado a que perdonemos a otros. "No nos metas en tentación, mas líbranos" — una súplica de que Dios nos guarde y nos rescate. Note el orden, porque es lo opuesto de como a muchos se les enseña: la adoración y la voluntad de Dios vienen primero; nuestras propias necesidades y nuestra confesión vienen después. No comenzamos con nuestra lista de peticiones, sino con nuestro Dios.

blocks.en: III. The Many Kinds of Prayer
blocks.es_reference: III. Las Muchas Clases de Oración

blocks.en: The Bible shows that prayer is not one single thing but many. There is praise and adoration, telling God how great and holy He is. There is thanksgiving, thanking Him for what He has done. There is confession: the Greek word means literally "to say the same thing" — in confession we agree with God about our sin, as the tax collector who cried, "God, be merciful to me a sinner!" (Luke 18:13, NKJV). There is supplication, which asks God to change our circumstances, yet even more to change our hearts, as the Lord Himself prayed in the garden, "not as I will, but as You will" (Matthew 26:39, NKJV). There is intercession, standing between God and others to pray for their needs — as Jesus prayed even for those who crucified Him, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do" (Luke 23:34, NKJV). We may also ask for ourselves; this is not a lack of faith but obedience, for Scripture says plainly, "you do not have because you do not ask" (James 4:2, NKJV). We may bring our honest questions to God, who is patient with all who sincerely seek to understand Him. And when we are so overwhelmed that we do not know what to pray, there is the prayer of groanings: "the Spirit Himself makes intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered" (Romans 8:26, NKJV). After all our words, there remains the prayer of listening — being still before God.
blocks.es_reference: La Biblia muestra que la oración no es una sola cosa, sino muchas. Está la alabanza y adoración, decirle a Dios cuán grande y santo es. Está la gratitud, darle gracias por lo que ha hecho. Está la confesión: la palabra griega significa literalmente "decir lo mismo" — en la confesión estamos de acuerdo con Dios acerca de nuestro pecado, como el publicano que clamó: "Dios, sé propicio a mí, pecador" (Lucas 18:13, RVG). Está la súplica, que pide a Dios que cambie nuestras circunstancias, pero aún más que cambie nuestro corazón, como el Señor mismo oró en el huerto: "no sea como yo quiero, sino como tú" (Mateo 26:39, RVG). Está la intercesión, ponerse entre Dios y otros para orar por sus necesidades — como Jesús oró aun por los que lo crucificaban: "Padre, perdónalos, porque no saben lo que hacen" (Lucas 23:34, RVG). También podemos pedir para nosotros mismos; esto no es falta de fe sino obediencia, pues la Escritura dice claramente: "no tenéis, porque no pedís" (Santiago 4:2, RVG). Podemos traer a Dios nuestras honestas preguntas, pues Él es paciente con todos los que sinceramente buscan entenderlo. Y cuando estamos tan abrumados que no sabemos qué orar, está la oración de gemidos: "el Espíritu mismo intercede por nosotros con gemidos indecibles" (Romanos 8:26, RVG). Después de todas nuestras palabras, queda la oración de escuchar — estar quietos delante de Dios.

blocks.en: Conclusion
blocks.es_reference: Conclusión

blocks.en: Prayer, then, is not a religious form but a living communication with a holy and loving Father — far more than conversation, yet carried on like one; ordered as the Lord taught us, with God first and our needs after; and rich in its many kinds, from praise to groaning to silent listening. In the next unit we will see how the saints and the Psalms prayed, how the church prays together, and how prayer is joined to fasting — and we will learn to pray expecting that our God hears and answers.
blocks.es_reference: La oración, entonces, no es una forma religiosa sino una comunicación viva con un Padre santo y amoroso — mucho más que una conversación, y sin embargo llevada a cabo como una; ordenada como el Señor nos enseñó, con Dios primero y nuestras necesidades después; y rica en sus muchas clases, desde la alabanza hasta el gemido y el escuchar en silencio. En la unidad siguiente veremos cómo oraron los santos y los Salmos, cómo ora junta la iglesia, y cómo se une la oración al ayuno — y aprenderemos a orar esperando que nuestro Dios oye y responde.

sa.prompt: How does Dr. Ted Rogers define prayer, and why is it more than 'simply a conversation'?
sa.model: Dr. Ted Rogers defines prayer as initiating communication with God for the purpose of intercession, supplication, praise, confession, and thanksgiving, with worshipful intent. It is more than 'simply a conversation' because it is initiated by us toward God alone (not the universe or created things), it is directed to Him with worshipful intent, and it changes us as we pray.

sa.prompt: Why must prayer be directed to God and not to 'the universe' or created things? (Use Genesis 4:26.)
sa.model: Prayer must be directed to God because the universe is made, but God is self-existent — praying to a created thing confuses the Creator with the creation. Already in the days of Enosh, men began to call on the name of the Lord (Genesis 4:26), showing that true prayer has always been directed to the one true God by name, with worshipful intent, not to any created thing.

sa.prompt: Although prayer is more than a conversation, how should we actually speak to God, and why?
sa.model: Though prayer is more than a mere conversation, it should be carried on like one — speaking to God plainly and honestly, as to a friend who loves us, rather than reaching for stiff, artificial, or overly formal words. God does not prefer a special religious language; He wants our natural, honest words.

sa.prompt: Why is the Lord's Prayer a model rather than words to repeat? (Use Matthew 6:7.)
sa.model: The Lord's Prayer is a model rather than words to repeat because Jesus had just warned, 'when you pray, do not use vain repetitions as the heathen do' (Matthew 6:7). He said 'in this manner, therefore, pray' — giving a pattern to follow, not a magic formula to recite mechanically.

sa.prompt: Explain 'Our Father' (abba) and 'hallowed be Your name.' What two things do they hold together?
sa.model: 'Our Father' uses abba, the most intimate family word of that day, so we come as a trusting child to a loving father. Yet 'hallowed be Your name' reminds us He is holy, set apart, utterly unique. Together they hold intimacy and reverence — closeness to God without losing awe of His holiness.

sa.prompt: What is striking about the ORDER of the Lord's Prayer?
sa.model: What is striking about the order of the Lord's Prayer is that God's kingdom and will come first — before any request for ourselves. Only halfway through do we ask for daily bread, and our own needs and confession come after adoration, which is the opposite of how many are taught to pray, starting with their own requests.

sa.prompt: Explain confession: what does the word mean, and what is required along with it?
sa.model: Confession literally means 'to say the same thing' — in confession we agree with God about our sin, as the tax collector who cried, 'God, be merciful to me a sinner!' (Luke 18:13). Along with confessing our own sin, Scripture ties our being forgiven to our forgiving others, as in the Lord's Prayer: 'forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.'

sa.prompt: What is the difference between supplication and intercession? Give an example of each.
sa.model: Supplication asks God to change our circumstances, yet even more to change our own heart, as Jesus prayed in the garden, 'not as I will, but as You will' (Matthew 26:39). Intercession stands between God and others, praying for their needs, as Jesus prayed even for those crucifying Him, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do' (Luke 23:34) — supplication centers on our own heart and circumstances, intercession on others.

sa.prompt: Is it right to ask God for our own needs? Why? (Use James 4:2 and the persistent widow.)
sa.model: Yes, it is right to ask God for our own needs; this is not a lack of faith but obedience, for Scripture says plainly, 'you do not have because you do not ask' (James 4:2). Jesus' parable of the persistent widow teaches the same lesson — that we should ask, and keep asking, trusting God as our faithful Provider rather than holding back out of false humility.

sa.prompt: Which kind of prayer (praise, confession, supplication, intercession, questions, groanings, listening) do you most need to grow in, and why?
sa.model: This is a personal reflection question inviting the student to consider which kind of prayer — praise, confession, supplication, intercession, honest questions, groanings, or listening — they most need to grow in. A thoughtful answer names a specific kind and explains why, based on their own walk with God and where it currently feels thin or underdeveloped.
